extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, patent examiners, inventors, and law students
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on what inventions may be joined in one patent application and detailed rules for preparing the specification (description and claims), including enablement, required contents, and form. Focuses on joinder of inventions (machines, processes, products, compositions, designs, improvements) and the substantive requirements of the description and claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Joinder of process and product
rubrics_metrics.description: A process and the article produced by it are distinct subjects and generally should be presented in separate applications; they cannot be joined unless inseparable or one necessarily implies the other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the process and product are inseparable (the product can only be produced by that process or the process cannot be conceived without the product) they may be joined; if the product can be produced by other processes, they should be separate. Office precedents (e.g., Ex parte Stow, O'Neill) illustrate the line. If another process is required to complete the product, they cannot be joined.

rubrics_metrics.name: Joinder of machines and their parts/sub-combinations
rubrics_metrics.description: A machine and its integral parts, or a machine and the product or process it performs, are proper subjects for a single patent when they are inseparable or when one cannot reasonably be contemplated as operative without the other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patent Office rules generally require a separate application for each machine unless: (a) one cannot be an operative instrument without the other, or (b) they constitute elements/sub-combinations of a principal machine. Parts may be separately patented, but the Office allows joining when parts cooperate to produce a single, unitary result; subordinate devices can be joined with the principal device. Cases cited include Wheeler v. McCormick, Excelsior Needle Co., Ex parte Wintherlich, Cobb.

rubrics_metrics.name: Joinder when machine, process and product are inseparable
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a machine, its process, and its product are inseparable as concrete inventions (each implies the other), they may be united in one patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the machine can only operate by producing the product and the product can only be produced by that machine, joinder is permitted (see Ex parte Wintherlich, Ex parte Cobb). Conversely, when separable they should be separate applications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Joinder of manufactures (products)
rubrics_metrics.description: Two manufactures may be joined when they are appropriate for use in the same article, serve a common purpose, or stand to each other as a combination and its elements; one may be joined if intrinsically dependent on the other or if one is the genus and the other a species.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Patent Office applies the same restrictions as for machines: one must be dependent on the other and co-operate to a unitary result. When a manufacture results from a new process or machine, joinder may be allowed, but the Office is cautious to prevent improper aggregations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Joinder of compositions of matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Compositions follow the same joinder rules as manufactures: independent compositions cannot be joined; those that cooperate to a common end or are elements/sub-combinations may be joined.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because every composition is a combination, its elements and sub-combinations may be joined with it. The Patent Office limits joinder of a composition with a machine or process to cases where they are inseparable. Example caution: one composition should not simply contain another with added ingredients.

rubrics_metrics.name: Joinder of designs
rubrics_metrics.description: Due to the character of designs, generally only one separate design can be included in a patent; subordinate elements that form a new design may be included, but multiple independent designs cannot be joined.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A design cannot be simultaneously protected as a manufacture and as a design in one patent. The Office disallows joining elements of a design with the design itself; modifications that do not affect identity are acceptable. Cases: Ex parte Gerard, Ex parte Patitz.

rubrics_metrics.name: Joinder of improvements
rubrics_metrics.description: Improvements may be joined when they are directly dependent on one another or indirectly related through dependence on the same original invention; independent improvements in distinct arts or unrelated machines cannot be joined.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Improvements that mutually cooperate to produce a given result or that increase joint efficiency can be united in one application. The Office forbids joinder unless one improvement depends on the other such that their cooperation is inevitable. Claims covering several distinct improvements relating to one article are not allowed (court may require disclaimers or division). See Burke v. Partridge, Sessions v. Romadka, Ex parte Herr.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to divide application when distinct inventions embraced
rubrics_metrics.description: If an application embraces distinct inventions that cannot properly be joined, the application must be divided into separate applications for each invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: On division, disclaimers must be filed with each division excluding matter not claimed therein. Once division is made excluded matter generally cannot be reinstated. Inventor may amend by striking out unjoinable inventions and filing separate applications; amendments may be ordered before final grant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification as contract and its twofold object
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification is a contract between the inventor and the public: in exchange for exclusive use it must (1) place the invention fully within public knowledge and (2) define the exact limits of the exclusive use to be protected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All rules governing specifications aim to secure these two objectives. The specification becomes part of the patent and fixes rights and public knowledge; completeness and accuracy are essential for validity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Division of specification into Description and Claim and their functions
rubrics_metrics.description: A specification has two parts: the Description (to communicate the invention to the public) and the Claim (to define the limits of the exclusive right).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Description may include broader contextual material and explanations; the Claim enumerates essential characteristics and refers to the Description for fuller explanation. The Claim is the measure of the patent; courts will not search the specification to supply definiteness the Claim should provide.

rubrics_metrics.name: Description: completeness and enablement requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: The Description must be so complete, clear, and exact that a person skilled in the art can make, construct, and use the invention during the life of the patent and enable public use after expiry without exercising inventive skill.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defective Descriptions that fail to enable are fatal; the degree of definiteness may vary by nature of invention but must be sufficient. Cases: Parks v. Booth, Wayne v. Holmes. The Office and courts require full disclosure of substance and form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Description must disclose invention, manner of making, and mode of use
rubrics_metrics.description: Statutorily the Description must contain full explanations of (1) the invention itself, (2) the manner of making/constructing it, and (3) the mode of putting it to practical use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each essential part must be clearly and exactly delineated and the relation of parts portrayed. The Description should state the best known mode of construction and operation. Failure on these points renders the specification defective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Description must explain principle and means, not merely results or modes
rubrics_metrics.description: A Description must explain the principle or means of the invention; a mere recital of the mode of using or a description of the result does not constitute an adequate description of the invention itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Descriptions of using an invention or of achieved results are insufficient unless they disclose the means/principle enabling reproduction (see Ex parte Doten, Burrall v. Ramsey). The description should reveal the idea of means rather than only the scientific principle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Description must disclose material properties when utility depends on them
rubrics_metrics.description: When the utility of the invention depends on some property of matter (e.g., a chemical property), the Description must describe that property to render the invention available.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the invention's operation is dependent on qualities of a produced article, the patentee is bound by the actual qualities existing in the produced article. Examples: Andrews v. Hovey, Goodyear v. New York Gutta Percha Co.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims must particularly and distinctly define the invention
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims must point out particularly and distinctly the invention to be secured; the Claim is the measure of the patent and must define essential characteristics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While the Description explains, the Claim delimits; a Claim cannot be vague. Both Description and Claims are required; the Claim may need to be specific and well-defined to supplement the Description (see Ex parte Skinner, Smith v. Murray).

rubrics_metrics.name: Both Description and Claims required in a specification
rubrics_metrics.description: A valid specification requires both a Description and at least one Claim; the Description alone is not sufficient under current statute—claims must supplement the description.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The primary object is description, but the Claim must specifically and distinctly define the invention. The patent office assumes specification parts will conform to statutes and rules; failure to include both may render application defective (see Ex parte Crandall).

rubrics_metrics.name: Office/court deference and difficulty applying joinder rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Although the joinder rules are theoretically clear, applying them to practical inventions is often difficult and may lead to disputes between inventors and the Patent Office; the Office's determination is ultimately controlling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the Office finds improper joinder, it may require division or refusal; inventors may amend by striking out or filing separate applications with disclaimers. Practical obscurities about relations between inventions frequently give rise to such conflicts.
